props.text: 1 The medical interview by Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 The medical interview • Define interviewing. • Illustrate different aims of an interview. • Discuss how to conduct a clinical interview • Apply the CLASS: The five key steps for clinical interviews Definition Interviewing is the interchange of verbal and non -verbal communication between two persons or more for the express intent of exchanging information and data relevant to the topics under consideration. Excellent communication skills provide us with the capacity to improve the quality and efficiency of the clinical care we can provide, while simultaneously making us more valuable team leaders and team members in healthcare. In addition to the shortened time to reach diagnosis and the resulting decreased resource utilization, there is an important business benefit achieved with improved communication The medical interview is probably the most important and most frequently used clinical tool. However, interviewing is also one of the most difficult clinical skills to master. The clinical encounter with the patient -and often the family- has four specific aims: • To gather information from the patient for determining the clinical diagnosis. • To transmit information to the patient in order to communicate the treatment plan. • To build a relationship in order to establish rapport and trust. • To support the patient and his family through the crisis of his illness. Regardless of whether medical improvement is possible, accomplishment of these goals can produce amelioration of the patient’s subjective symptoms. Communication skills are essential for both. Medical interviewing is a core medical skill. Medical interview is the major medium of care because: • It determines the problems addressed. • It forms the doctor-patient relationship. • It determines knowledge of the life context of the illness which may give clues to causes of the disease and its management. • It is the medium of patient education about the different aspects of the disease, its etiology, prevention, diagnostic procedures and therapy. Moreover, it is a tool for orienting the patient about what behaviors he should do to deal with his condition. Opening the interview Beginning of the interview: introduction and listening: The beginning of an interview is a powerful time to make important first impressions, establish rapport, and identify problems that set the tone for the entire relationship. Preparation prior to the interview is important. • It is not uncommon to be mentally focusing on the last task or last patient, or perhaps thinking of your own personal needs, creating a situation such that your attention is not fully focused on the upcoming new patient. Distraction hampers effective communication. your body language often betrays this distraction, and may set the wrong impression. You must allow yourself to be free to concentrate on your upcoming patient. Stopping to take a 3 deep breath before knocking may allow you to recenter yourself on the upcoming encounter and give it your undivided attention. • The simple act of waiting after knocking i nstead of knocking and then entering immediately is a common courtesy, which although it delays an additional second, it sets a tone of respect. 1. Introduce yourself: Before starting the interview, itself: • Know who the patient is before you walk through the door. • Human beings love the sound of their own name. It is believed to be the most important word for each individual. At a minimum, clinicians must use the patient’s name at the beginning and the end of the visit. Using a patient’s name avoids errors and is a sure way to clarify that you are with the right patient. In addition, it indicates your respect for that particular individual. Once you are in front of the patient: • Try to be relaxed, have a confident smile make and maintain eye contact and most commonly shake hands and introduce yourself and sit upright. The non -verbal greeting (Your own facial expressions and patients' facial expressions may give clues regarding things they are not saying, as well as alert you to pain and severity of pain. Facial expressions may also allow you to see to what degree you are connecting with your patients) occurs before the actual verbal introduction. • Then clarifying your role as a caregiver can be incredibly helpful in new encounters. This is especially beneficial in the inpatient setting, where multiple caregivers are involved and each one’s role is not as clear. Example: ‘Hello, Mr. Green, I’m Dr. Smith. I will be the senior doctor seeing you during your stay in the hospital. Can I spend a few minutes with you now discussing your problems and examining you?’ Physician: "Good morning, Haj My name is Ahmed Ali. I am the doctor of this ward." Medical Student: "Good morning, Set Om Ahmed. My name is Ossama Ibrahim. I am a medical student." 2. Establish aims of the interview: Health history interviews are of two basic types; the problem -oriented and the health promotion interviews. In reality most of them combine the two types. The aims of problem -oriented interview reflect the patient's request for help with specific problems. The health promotion interviews establish a data baseline concerning the person's current and past health problems, assesses current health risk factors (heritable diseases, family history, smoking, diet, exercise, drug substance etc.). They can detect early evidence of disease (chest pain, weight loss, change in bowel habits etc.). Whatever the type of the interview is, there is a need to brief the patient about the purpose and the expectation of the interview. Examples Physician: "Good morning, Haj My name is Ahmed Ali. I am the doctor of this ward. I need to take a detailed history of your condition". 4 Medical Student: "Good morning, Set Om Ahmed. My name is Osama Ibrahim. I am a medical student learning how to interview patients. The doctor gave me your name." 3. Obtain patient consent: Informed consent is both an ethical obligation and a legal requirement. It is central to the practice of good medicine. It is a necessary component of the patients' ability to make decisions about what is best for them. For most interviews in actual practice, patient consent is implied by the patient’s presence in the physician’s office or hospital. However, it can be helpful to ask the patient permission to discuss their personal health information prior to jumping into an interview. 4. Establishing Initial Rapport: Establishing rapport may be the most important part of the interview. The doctor -patient relationship begins at the moment the physician and the patient see each other, even before any words are uttered (تُنطقThe patient and the physician will each make many judgments about the other before they establish verbal contact. Body posture, eye contact, interest level, and numerous other nonverbal cues will communicate important information to both the patient and the doctor. • Listen carefully and do not interrupt your patient. • Focus on the patient and maintain eye contact. • Be reliable and don’t make unrealistic promises. • Show support: smile and touch when appropriate. Signs of Improved Rapport • Increased flow of conversation. • Disclosure of sensitive information. • Relaxed body language. • Increased eye contact. • Better listening and responding. In general, the key to rapport is to demonstrate interest in the patient as a person. This can be demonstrated by showing concern and attention. Appearing hurried, bored, exhausted, or distracted can seriously undermine the relationship with the patient. You have to be able to identify signs of poor rapport which are: • Long period of silence. • Sudden withdrawal from conversation. • Lack of eye contact. • Brief responses. • Defensive body language. 5 To sets out a basic and practical approach for acquiring and improving effective communication

props.text: Introduction To Communication BY PROF. DR. SOMAYA MADKOUR Forensic Medicine and Clinical Toxicology Department Read the following SLOs Listen & comment Communication T he imparting or exchanging of information by speaking, writing, or using some other medium. If this recipient does not understand and interpret the message the way it was intended, then that constitutes… FAILURE OF COMMUNICATION Communication Shared opinion Personal knowledge Personal knowledge Effective communication Environment Culture Participants Doctor patient Relation Source Encoding Channel Decoding Receiver Feedback Message Message Context Message Message Message Message Source A managing physician must always be in control of the sources of information that the patient is exposed to. The best way to do this is by having a clear and open channel of communication with the patient. This way the patient will check with his physician every time he hears or reads something and want to further inquire about. Encoding When communicating a message to a layperson about his condition or treatment it is inappropriate to use any medical jargon or terms. However, when communicating the same message to a patient who is a physician it is inappropriate to NOT speak in medical terms. This is an example of why considering the language, tone, emotion, and content of the message should be accurately tailored to each patient. Consider the same message being delivered to a child, an intellectually challenged patient, a deaf-mute patient, an elderly patient…. etc Decoding Despite your best efforts in encoding a message properly, it is still unclear how the patient will perceive this message. Patient’s perception can be influenced by their past experiences and external influences. A physician with good communication skills will always explore these two areas and relate to how they may influence their patients. Feedback Feedback is a very important tool for physicians to be sure they delivered the message accurately and also to ensure that they understand the messages from the patients. Patient understands the physician’s explanation, rationale, and recommendation Feedback Physician understands patient complaints, needs, concerns, and decisions Context The final item to consider is the context of the communication process. These are a group of factors external to the patient and that strongly influence the communication process. The most important such factors are: The environment where the communication process is taking place, e.g. emergency room versus outpatient clinic The patient’s culture. E.g. rural versus urban cultures . Participants in the process. E.g. translators for foreign patients, parents of a child, children on an elderly patient . Relation between physician and patient. Suppose Andrew wants to invite his friend or friends to hang out in his house. Now since this will be on short notice, he needs to make a message and choose the medium for the message to reach his friends as soon as possible. Slow medium will not let him achieve his goal so that he will opt for quicker options. Now it’s either So, texting or calling his friends. Now, if he chooses to text every single friend of his, then all of them might read the text at a different time and miss out on the invitation. he will have to call everyone up to see who’s available. Then he has to make sure the other person is free to make the invitation to. To invite them, he has to maintain a friendly tone because they are coming for a relaxed hour. Hence, he calls up everyone to see I they are busy or not and then invites them over. He analysis if the friend who just had a breakup would like to join or not, the friend with family problems might just run to his house to spend a more relaxed time. Because of this choice of mode medium and considerations, many of his friends got to enjoy themselves with him. This tells how the ripple effects start, just the thought being communicated and put to action. Brenda wants to remind her husband, Roberto, to stop by the store after work and buy milk for dinner. She forgot to ask him in the morning, so Brenda texts a reminder to Roberto. He texts back and then shows up at home with a gallon of milk under his arm. But something's amiss: Roberto bought chocolate milk when Brenda wanted regular milk. In this example, the sender is Brenda. The receiver is Roberto. The medium is a text message. The code is the English language they're using. And the message itself is "Remember the milk!" In this case, the feedback is both direct and indirect. Roberto texts a photo of milk at the store (direct) and then came home with it (indirect). However, Brenda did not see the photo of the milk because the message didn't transmit (noise) and Roberto didn't think to ask what kind of milk (context). What do we communicate FEELING IDEA INFORMATION ATTIUDE VALUE BEHAVIOR Think about this patient A 21-year-old drug addict is presented to you at the PHC clinic where you are the on-duty GP. You have nothing to lose if you try to quit everything now IDEA INFORMATION Drugs are not that harmful . I will never die because I don’t OD 2.5% of IV users die/year Many deaths are caused by BE, HIV, and HBV. A lot of people who OD do not do it intentionally Everyone uses drugs. (Apathy) This condition is cause for concern and worry. (anxiety) You could’ve been much better. (anger) You should have hope that you can quit one day. (hope) FEELING I will never be able to beat addiction I’m not an addict, I can stop anytime You should try and look for help wherever you can get it. Drugs make me look cool Addiction only affects me Think how much you are hurting your family. VALUE You should start seeking help I am going to continue using drugs Importance of good communication Build rapport Define and understand goals. Receive and share information Promote self-confidence Avoid negative effects of conflict and confusion Now you try this one out A 43-year-old police officer, married, has 3 children, He is a heavy smoker (2 packs/day, smoking index 850) He has positive family history (uncles and grandfather) of dyslipidemia, DM, CHD, and sudden death. He comes to your PHC unit. He is outraged, calls you a butcher, says his father lived till he was 87 with no problem despite having the same circumstances (occupation, smoking, family history) Not all family member should catch the disease Nothing will happen . Next time it will pass & I will be safe . I will be like my father You have many risk factors for heart disease including stressful work, smoking, family history, age, gender, not counting that you already had chest pain, and ECG changes My father lived till he was 87 with no problem despite having the same circumstances (occupation, smoking, family history) The “heart disease” genes may have skipped your father but still passed to you Smokers have a higher heart disease risk than never-smokers, and two to three times the risk of death. The more you smoke, the higher your risk of death . You had a relative who died suddenly, do you think this may happen to you? It happens to any person No one dies (Denial) Ignoring your health is very irresponsible and possibly even sinful Feeling Everyone dies anyway. (Apathy) Cigarette smoking cost a lot of money. Establish aims of the interview Health history interviews are of two basic types; the problem-oriented and the health promotion interviews. In reality most of them combine the two types. The aims of problem-oriented interview reflect the patient's request for help with specific problems. The health promotion interviews establish a data baseline concerning the person's current and past health problems, assesses current health risk factors (heritable diseases, family history, smoking, diet, exercise, drug substance etc.). They can detect early evidence of disease (chest pain, weight loss, change in bowel habits etc.). Whatever the type of the interview is, there is a need to brief the patient about the purpose and the expectation of the interview 3. Obtain patient consent Informed consent is both an ethical obligation and a legal requirement. It is central to the practice of good medicine. It is a necessary component of the patients' ability to make decisions about what is best for them. For most interviews in actual practice, patient consent is implied by the patient’s presence in the physician’s office or hospital. However, it can be helpful to ask the patient permission to discuss their personal health information prior to jumping into an interview. 4.Establishing Initial Rapport Establishing rapport may be the most important part of the interview. The doctor-patient relationship begins at the moment the physician and the patient see each other, even before any words are uttered ( تُنطق ) The patient and the physician will each make many judgments about the other before they establish verbal contact. Body posture, eye contact, interest level, and numerous other nonverbal cues will communicate important information to both the patient and the doctor. In general, the key to rapport is to demonstrate interest in the patient as a person. This can be demonstrated by showing concern and attention. Appearing hurried, bored, exhausted, or distracted can seriously undermine the relationship with the patient. The five key steps for clinical interviews is easy to remember and to use in practice C L A S S C-Context (setting) “A private area with no distractions” Physical Space Student’ learning outcomes at the end of the session, you will be able to L- LISTENING SKILLS “Be an effective listener” After listening to what your patient said, You should ask him some questions . The questions should: •Use open-to-close ended cone approach. •First use open- ended questions in opening the interview and for opening new topics as they rise. These are nondirective questions. These questions will help patient to describe their problems according to their experience using their own language. They will help you to learn about environmental and other risk factors that may influence the development of symptoms. Also, it indicates the willingness of the doctor to listen to his patient. Example Dr. : What symptoms brought you to hospital today? After an initial nondirective phase, the doctor must ask progressively more focused questions to explore specific diagnostic hypothesis. So, he uses closed-ended questions. Example Dr. : Where is the pain? Dr. : Is the pain sharp? •Use enough facilitation. Use comments to encourage your patient to keep talking Example Dr. : Tell me more about this colic. Dr. : Can you describe more your headache. A- ACKNOWLEDGE EMOTIONS “Explore, identify, and respond to the emotion” The Empathic Response 1- Identify the emotion that the patient is experiencing. 2- Identify the cause of the emotion. 3-Respond by showing you have made the connection between the emotion and the cause e.g. “That must have felt terrible when...” or “Most people would be upset about this.” Definition: Interviewing is the interchange of verbal and non-verbal communication between two persons or more for the express intent of exchanging information and data relevant to the topics under consideration. S– STRATEGY “Propose a plan that the patient will understand” It is important to ensure that you construct a management plan that the patient will understand and follow. S- SUMMARY “ closing the interview” This particular part of the interview is not necessarily long, but it requires a considerable focus and concentration. • Summarize the discussion in a clear and concise manner. • Check the patient’s understanding. • Ask if the patient has any other questions for you. • If you don’t have time for further questions, suggest that they can be addressed at the next appointment. • Make a clear contract for a follow up visit. props.text: Dr Ahmed Elsheshai, MD MRCPsych elsheshai@yahoo.com Dr Ahmed Elsheshai, MD MRCPsych elsheshai@yahoo.com Abstract An overview of what it means to be a professional, who is considered a medical professional, the foundations of medical ethics, communications skills, and how to conduct oneself to the best interest of the patient and medical profession. Abstract An overview of what it means to be a professional, who is considered a medical professional, the foundations of medical ethics, communications skills, and how to conduct oneself to the best interest of the patient and medical profession. Medical profession MED131 Medical profession MED131 L1: Introduc tion & Overview of Professionalism Part 1: What is professionalism The competences expected of a professional Competence = skill + knowledge + experience Thinking about your studies in medical school, reflect on how you are working to gain knowledge, skill, and experience to become a medical professional According to the American board of internal medicine, the competencies expected of a physician are: “ A spiring toward altruism, accountability, excellence, duty, service, honor, integrity, and respect for others.” Altruism ( الإيثار ): The only productive outcome of our work as physicians is improving patients’ quality of life. Therefore, this should be our prime target and we should aim to achieve everything else only through the poatient’s benefit and never despite of it. Accountability ( المساءلة ): Whether before he makes them, while he makes them, or after he makes them, a physician should always be ready and willing to be held accountable for his decisions. A physician’s will and acceptance of accountability at all stages of decision making signifies that all his decisions have only the best interest of the patient at heart and the best available evidence on his mind. Excellence ( التميز ): When have you ever heard of a patient settling for a mediocre doctor? In our time of weakness, we always seek the most excellent medical service we can have. It is essential that doctors provide a minimum level of excellence that assures that no matter where a patient might end up, they will have a satisfactory service provided to them. Duty ( الواجب ): The medical profession is not one that is bound by the rules of working hours or fees for service. Instead, medical professionals should be motivated in the first place by their sense of duty and responsibility towards their patients. Service ( الخدمة ): Medical professionals work in the service of their patients. All actions that a physician makes in his career should be geared towards this prime and only target. Hono u r ( الشرف ): A physician’s actions should always be honorable. Meaning that he/she should always be doing what he/she knows and believes to be the morally correct action. Integrity ( النزاهة ): While “honour” means knowing and intending to do well, “integrity” means actually doing the honourable action, being honest about it, and having a clear, constant, and honourable direction for their actions. Respect for others ( احترام الآخرين ): The medical profession is a very busy one. While in other professions one may deal with only his client and maybe a few colleagues, physicians deal with so many stakeholders every single day. Patients, relatives, caregivers, colleagues, managers, seniors, and junior doctors just to name a few. In dealing with all these people, doctors should have respect for the diversity of their views, backgrounds , and intentions. Of course, and above all, respect for patients reign supreme. Part 2: The social contract The relation of the medical field with society is an especially complicated one. Doctors usually view treating patients and dealing with the hardships of a disease in a very practical way as their everyday job. Patients suffering from this disease regard this matter with more emotionality and sensitivity. To achieve a balance between these two contradicting views, a social contract was outlined to describe what society should expect from doctors and vice versa. Society’s expectations from medicine The service of a healer : society expects doctors to understand that the primary target for all their actions is healing patients. Assured competence : Either because it is too difficult or impractical, patients cannot test their doctors’ knowledge and skill before accepting their services. Therefore, it is the duty of the medical community to assure that those working in this profession have the necessary and essential set of skills and knowledge to carry their jobs properly. Altruistic service : As mentioned earlier, doctors should only seek success through their patients’ well-being. A patient giving himself in to his doctor should trust that the doctor only has his best interest at heart. Morality and integrity: patients need to trust that doctors are acting according to the best-known standards and that what doctors do to them is the same as what would be done to the doctors if they were in their shoes. Accountability : Again, as patients’ do not usually have medical education, it is their right to be able to hold physicians accountable for their actions. This is not a thing that physicians should shy from, instead a physician should always be ready to defend his/her decisions and actions. Transparency : Physicians should be clear about all forces influencing their decisions. Whether there is a conflict of interest or whether th ere is something a patient may object to, it is not a physician’s right to hide anything from their patient. 1 : while many patients value their doctors’ personal opinions, it is imperative that physicians provide impartial and objective advise based of the best known evidence. Moreover, when expressing their opinion, physicians should point this out clearly, explaining the difference between evidence and choice. Promotion of the public good : finally, physicians are expected to not only promote their individual patient’s health, but also the public good of all society and the prevention of all disease and suffering. Medical profession’s expectations from society Trust : While it is a patient’s right to know and understand everything he is going through, it is not always practical to explain every little detail about their illness and treatment. Therefore, doctors need society to trust them that they are doing what is best for the ir patients . Autonomy : in practicing medicine, doctors need to have autonomy and not to be forced to take any actions they believe is not in the best interest of their patients. Self-regulation : The medical profession is a complicated one, where many professionals work together and where the slightest margin of error can prove fatal. Therefore, regulating this delicate workplace should be left to those carrying this responsibility and who best understand it. A health care system that is value-driven and adequately funded : imagine a patient who has a problem in the arteries of his lower limbs (a condition called ischemia), he cannot walk properly and has started using a wheelchair. Which is a more proper target to describe this patient’s need: to be able to walk freely again (value), or to perform an operation on his arteries (service)? Sometimes just performing a service such as surgery, writing a prescription, or doing physiotherapy is not enough on its own to achieve the value that the patient needs. In a service-oriented healthcare system, patients provide fees and doctors provide service. However, in a value-based healthcare system, patients and doctors decide on a specific target value they want to achieve, then the doctors work with their teams and with the patient to achieve that target regardless of how many services will or will not be included. Both doctors and patients stand to have great benefit from having a value-based and well-funded healthcare system. props.text: Doctor-Patient Relationship Dr Ahmed Elsheshai MD MRCPsych Physicians act as “teachers” At the extreme, Physicians may engage with patients in “deliberation” of all available courses of action. E.g. Jehovah’s witnesses refuse blood transfusions, Muslims refuse wine as sleep aid, vegans may insist on a special diet, and someone may just value their temporary well-being over an extended life of sickness in refusing chemotherapy. Informative model (Consumer) The physician informs the patient of his/her disease state, the nature of possible therapeautic and diagnostic interventions, the nature and probability of risks and benefits associated with each intervention, and any uncertainties of knowledge. The patient selects the medical intervention he/she wants and the physician then proceeds to execute them. Physicians act as information vendors or technical expert. At the extreme , patients could come to know all medical information relevant to their disease and available interventions that best relaize their values. Especially valuable in chronic conditions requiring continuous care such as DM and RA, also in elective and aesthetic procedures. Interpretive model (Advocate) Here the physician tries to clarify the patient’s values, describe available intervention options in light of patient’s values, and help patients decide the best option that fits their values Physician act as counselor At the extreme , the physician will form a full picture of the patient’s life as a narrative whole and from this specify the patient’s values and what is best done to help. Examples where this model is especially effective include lifestyle medicine, dietary medicine, sport medicine, and addiction medicine. Paternalistic Deliberative Informative Interpretive Patient values Only concern is health, shared by physician & patient Open to development and revision Defined fixed and known to the patient. Require clarification and agreement Physician’s obligation Patient well-being independent of their prefernece Persuading the patient of the best path… and implement their choice. Provide factual information… and implement patient’s choice . Clarify patient’s personal values… and implement their choice. Autonomy Assenting to objective health values Developed through understanding of health values Control over medical care Developed through understanding of own values Physician role Guardian Teacher or friend Technical expert Counselor or advisor Impact of DPR Physicians who communicate well and treat patients with chronic illnesses fairly improve the patient’s ability to manage their disease independently with adherence to the advice of doctors. For example, patients monitor their blood pressure and adhere to medical regimens as per the advice of the doctor to manage health disorders such as hypertension and diabetes. An “international footballer” who makes around $500K/week, sustains a knee injury. The radical intervention will allow him to return to field in 1 year therefore missing a whole seasons with his team. The alternative will allow him to return to the field in 3 months, but he has to take intensive physiotherapy and in around 3 years he probably will need knee replacement. Brain-storm Who would act in a paternalistic model? Who would act as a deliberative physician? Who would assume the informative model? Who may be the Interpretive doctor in this situation? A consensual relationship in which the patient knowingly seeks the physician’s assistance and in which the physician knowingly accepts the person as a patient. Thank you Matter in question Fundamentals of DPR 4 Models of DPR An “international footballer” who makes around $500K/week, sustains a knee injury. The radical intervention will allow him to return to field in 1 year therefore missing a whole seasons with his team. The alternative will allow him to return to the field in 3 months, but he has to take intensive physiotherapy and in around 3 years he probably will need knee replacement. Paternalistic model (Authoritarian) Physicians use their skills to determine the diagnosis, required investigations, and best treatment. Then they will present the patient with selected information that will encourage the patients to consent to the doctors opinion. This model assumes that the criteria for decision making is shared between patient and physician. i.e. no personal issues or choices. Physician act as guardian At the extreme , the physician only informs the patient when the intervention will be initiated. Usually only advocated in emergency situations and where patients are incapacitated (e.g. disoriented or severely psychotic patients). Deliberative model (Authoritative) Physicians recommend the course they see best and discuss with the patient why this course should be taken. The physician here should stick ONLY to health related values. i.e. values that affect or are affected by the patient’s disease or treatment. The patient feels empowered and safe in choosing a path that adheres to their health as well as life values.

props.text: Attributes of a Physician Dr Ahmed Elsheshai MD, MRCPsych Optimism Hopefulness and confidence about the future or the success of something. “Optimism is the faith that leads to achievement. Nothing is done without hope & confidence.” Communication skills The imparting or exchanging of information by speaking, writing, or using some other medium Good decisions can turn into disasters when communicated poorly Organization skills Organizational skills are a set of techniques used by an individual to facilitate the efficiency of future-oriented learning, problem-solving, and task completion. For every minute spent organizing, an hour is earned. Meticulous Showing great attention to detail; very careful and precise. Meticulous planning will enable everything a man does to appear spontaneous Curiosity A strong desire to know or learn something. Curiosity is one of the most permanent and certain characteristics of a vigorous intellect. Curiosity is the origin of knowledge; experience is the origin of wisdom. Collaboration The action of working with someone to produce something Collaboration – the ultimate intertwining of skill, passion, and knowledge – is what concocts the most shatter-proof forms of change-making Persistance Continuing in an opinion or course of action in spite of difficulty or opposition. Persistence guarantees that results are inevitable Compassion Sympathetic concern for the sufferings or misfortunes of others. Use what seems like poison as medicine. Use your personal suffering as the path to compassion for all beings. Confidence A feeling of trust in one's abilities, qualities, and judgement. A man cannot be comfortable without his own approval Humility The quality of having a modest or low view of one's importance. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. SLOs Passion Strong and barely controllable emotion. Skills are cheap, passion is priceless Mentorship The guidance provided by a mentor, especially an experienced person. In learning you will teach and in teaching you will learn. Courage The ability to do something that frightens one. Courage is grace under pressure Humanity The quality or state of being human. Believing in what sets humanity apart and makes humans special. The good physician treats the disease; the great physician treats the patient who has the disease. Build your character around your passion in this wonderful career. props.text: Overview and Development of Medical Ethics Dr Ahmed A Elsheshai Thomas Percival The four pillars of medical ethics Autonomy Beneficence Non-Maleficence Justice Consider the following case: A 52 year old man collapses in the street complaining of severe acute pain in his right abdomen. A surgeon happens to be passing and examines the man. Suspecting that he is on the brink of rupturing his appendix (a potentially life threatening condition), the surgeon decides the best course of action is to remove the appendix immediately, using his trusty pocket knife. Pause the video and debate the actions of the surgeon for a minute. how do the surgeon’s actions benefit the patient? And how do they harm him? Do you believe the surgeon took the best course of action? Beneficence “I will use treatment to benefit the sick according to my ability and judgement, but never with a view to injury and wrongdoing” Hippocrates It is the duty to try and bring about those improvements in physical or psychological health that medicine can achieve. E.g. giving the most effective antibiotics for an infection. Non malificence “First do no harm” Going about medical activities in ways that prevent further injury or reduce its risk. E.g. giving the antibiotic with the least side effects and least cost. 14 In the previous example: The surgeon’s action may save the patient’s life. According to the concept of beneficence, the surgeon is justified to take this line of action On the other hand, The environment is unlikely to be sterile, as is the pocket knife, so risk of infection is very high. There are no other medical staff or surgical equipment available, therefore chances that the operation will succeed are very narrow. The surgeon may have experience in performing appendectomy before, but definitely never on a street. Therefore experience is decontextualized and inappropriate. The weighing of these two points show that unless there is no hospital around for many miles, the actions of the surgeon are highly disproportionate. 15 Consider the following case: Ali is a patient suffering from repeated attacks of angina (mini-heart attacks). He is admitted to the hospital for followup, investigation, observation, and emergency intervention. Although there is an order for medication to treat his heart condition, Ali refuses these medications daily. On one visit, his family members notice that he is not taking his medications and demand that you hide them in his mashed potatoes. Pause the lecture and think about the best course of action. What if you refuse to trick him into taking the drugs and subsequently he deteriorates or even worse, suffers a major heart attack and dies? Autonomy Requires that the patient have autonomy of thought, intention, and action when making decisions regarding health care procedures. Therefore, the decision-making process must be free of coercion or coaxing. For a patient to make a fully informed decision, she/he must understand all risks and benefits of the procedure and the likelihood of success. Respect for autonomy is a two-way street The autonomy of a physician to act only on their best judgement about how to benefit the patient medically should be respected Therefore, respect for the patient autonomy does not imply that the patient has the right to demand inappropriate treatment or that the physician must accede to any and every request of a patient if it conflicts with the physician’s best judgement. 18 Justice The idea that the burdens and benefits of treatments must be distributed equally among all groups in society. Requires that procedures uphold the spirit of existing laws and are fair to all players involved. The health care provider must consider four main areas when evaluating justice: fair distribution of scarce resources competing needs rights and obligations potential conflicts with established legislation 19 Transfer goals To be able to understand the meaning of medical ethics, and the scope of the subject. To understand that medical ethics is not an intuitive quality in a physician, but rather a field of study that often requires a lot of deliberation to be navigated and used. Consider the following case: Patients suspected of having cancer are prioritised within the NHS, with the maximum waiting time for referral being two weeks (as opposed to 18 weeks for non-urgent referrals). Patients diagnosed with cancer are entitled to a range of treatments including radio- and chemotherapy. These treatments are expensive and treat a small, but significant proportion of patients. It could be argued that prioritising cancer patients means you’re limiting the ability of other patients to access healthcare. A counter-argument might be that by referring these patients to specialist oncology centres, you’re actually freeing up other services. Then again, spending public money on radio- and chemotherapy on a smaller group of people is taking budget away from less expensive treatments that would benefit a greater number of people – for example, insulin for diabetic patients. A counter-argument would be that early treatment increases survival rates and actually reduces the cost of cancer treatment Consider 3 healthcare systems… How is the principle of “justice” applied in each system? Take-home message Medical ethics: is a branch of bioethics is a precise field that strives to leave nothing to intuition Unlike moral philosophy which can be debated Has been a topic of interest for physicians eversince humanity knew medicine Thomas Percival’s outline of the 4 main pillars of ethics remain the quintessential & non-debatable laws of the subject. Which are: Beneficence: “I will do my best to benefit my patient” Non maleficence: “first, I will do no harm” Autonomy: “I will respect my patient’s free-will and choice” Justice: “I will make sure my care is accessible to all my patients equally” Thank you SLOs Define medical ethics and bioethics. Understand the 4 basic concepts of medical ethics Autonomy Beneficence Non-maleficence Justice Use principles of bioethics to solve hypothetical ethical dilemmas What is Medical Ethics? Dr Ahmed A Elsheshai, MD MRCPsych Psychiatry Consultant The story of medical ethics Medical Papyri The Egyptian physician made a prognosis before undertaking treatment. If the prognosis was favorable, the physician's comment was "an ailment that I shall treat"; if it was uncertain, "an ailment that I shall combat"; and if the prognosis was unfavorable, "an ailment not to be treated. (Left) Plates vi & vii of the Edwin Smith Papyrus at the Rare Book Room , New York Academy of Medicine. Hippocratic oath I swear by Apollo Healer, by Asclepius, by Hygieia , by Panacea, and by all the gods and goddesses, making them my witnesses, that I will carry out, according to my ability and judgment, this oath and this indenture. To hold my teacher in this art equal to my own parents ; to make him partner in my livelihood; when he is in need of money to share mine with him; to consider his family as my own brothers, and to teach them this art, if they want to learn it, without fee or indenture; to impart precept, oral instruction, and all other instruction to my own sons, the sons of my teacher, and to indentured pupils who have taken the Healer’s oath, but to nobody else. I will use those dietary regimens which will benefit my patients according to my greatest ability and judgment, and I will do no harm or injustice to them. Neither will I administer a poison to anybody when asked to do so, nor will I suggest such a course. Similarly I will not give to a woman a pessary to cause abortion. I will keep pure and holy both my life and my art. I will not use the knife, not even, verily, on sufferers from stone, but I will give place to such as are craftsmen therein. Into whatsoever houses I enter, I will enter to help the sick, and I will abstain from all intentional wrong-doing and harm, especially from abusing the bodies of man or woman, bond or free. props.text: Introduction and Overview of Professionalism Dr Ahmed A Elsheshai What is the scope of this subject? Scope of the course Good Medical Practice This phrase sets out the principles that characterise good medical practice and makes explicit the standards of professional conduct expected of doctors by their professional peers and the community. Traditional medical education focus on teaching medical students to become clinicians. That is the basic raw knowledge of disease and treatment. GMP focuses on how doctors use this information to help other humans restore their lives to the best possible quality. Good medical practice: a code of conduct for doctors in Australia Professionalism and ethics handbook for residents: a practical guide (Saudi commission for health specialties) Medical Ethics I s an applied branch of the philosophy of ethics which analyses the practice of clinical medicine and related scientific research. The term was first coined by British author and physician “Thomas Percival in 1803. However, the formal practice of describing the ethics of the profession of medicine date back to the Hippocratic oath back in the 4 th century BC. Communication Skills from Latin communicare , meaning "to share" or "to be in relation with" Quality One notable and widely used definition is “ making sure that all activities are carried out in the right manner the first time and every time . ” Institute of Medicine’s six domains to measure and describe quality of care in health: safe – avoiding injuries to patients from care that is intended to help them effective – avoiding overuse and misuse of care patient-Centered – providing care that is unique to a patient's needs timely – reducing wait times and harmful delays for patients and providers efficient – avoiding waste of equipment, supplies, ideas and energy equitable – providing care that does not vary across intrinsic personal characteristics Can you find an argument AGAINST… Good medical practice? right to profession role as leader of the medical team Ethical practice? Doctor’s personal values Doctor’s superior knowledge Good communication? Scarce resources Time management Quality practice? Scarce resources Financial gain Can you think of an example for these arguments? props.text: 1 Communication by Dr/ Somaya Madkour Professor of Forensic Medicine & Clinical Toxicology Alexandria University 2 Communication ILOs ▪ Explain the differences between written and oral communication. ▪ List types of written communication in health care setting. ▪ Define nonverbal communication. ▪ Describe the main functions of nonverbal communication. ▪ List types of nonverbal communication. ▪ Describe each type. Communication is a process by which information is transferred or exchanged between people through a common system of symbols, signs, or behavior. In the medical field, the whole practice of medicine relies heavily on communication. It is done for, swapping of ideas, delivering messages, and exchanging information through signals, speech, or writings. • Seeing: Deliver 55% of the message. It is seen or felt and consists of facial expression, dress, grooming, posture, eye contact, touch, and gesture • Hearing: the heard voice that depends on the tone, vocal clarity, and verbal expressiveness. It delivers 38% of the message • The words by themselves delivering only 7% of the message Mark Twain, a famous American poet-writer, said, “If we were supposed to talk more than listen, we would have been given two mouths and one ear.” Doctors, while communicating with their patients, should master both the tongue and the body language. Usually, all forms of communication tools internally and externally are used while conducting a consultation. Having strong communication skills is essential for building both personal and professional relationships. There are two predominant types of communication: verbal and nonverbal. While most of us are aware of and use verbal communication on a regular basis, nonverbal communication is most commonly not intentional and can offer considerable information about both people and situations. Types of Communication 1. Verbal oral Communication Oral communication refers to the spoken words in the communication process. It can be a talk with or without illustrations. The audience listens and watches the verbal presentation of information given by the speaker. There are a large number of different verbal oral communication skills. They range from the obvious (being able to speak clearly, or listening, for example), to the more subtle (such as reflecting and clarifying). Examples of oral Communication ▪ Face-to-face conversation 3 ▪ Giving a speech (lecture & seminars) ▪ Telephonic conversation ▪ Sending voice note over the internet ▪ Taking interviews ▪ Group discussion in workplace ▪ Thesis defense Verbal communication skills There are basically two communication skills widely accepted. They are known as Effective speaking and active listening. • Effective speaking involves how well we choose our words. • Active listening involves how patiently we hear others. • These factors affect the transmission of messages. • Saves a lot of time and money. • These skills bring a positive response. Components of verbal communication • Pitch of the voice • Speed of the voice • Tone • Language • Grammar Advantages of oral Communication ▪ It saves a lot of time, money and energy. ▪ There are fewer chances of confusion because of clarity of method. ▪ The information conveyed in verbal communication is easy to understand, as the doubts are cleared immediately. ▪ Feedback is got quickly once a message is delivered. ▪ It is a very reliable form of communication and thus people prefer it worldwide over other types of communication. ▪ Verbal communication is the most convenient method of communication for its straightforward and understandable quality. ▪ Any person who can speak a language can easily communicate verbally and does not need any material to convey the messages. Disadvantages of Verbal Communication 1. Language differences – If the receiver is unaware of the sender’s language, then communication cannot be carried out. So, difference in language and dialect is a big barrier in the path of effective communication. 2. Lack of records – There is no means of recording the information permanently unless any modern device of storage is used. Hence, one cannot refer to the communication later on. 3. Unsuitable for long messages – When a lengthy message is to be imparted, then this form of communication is not at all suitable. The important points may be missed out and the lengthy paragraphs may cause misinterpretation by the receiver. 4. Communication-gap – While conveying messages orally several irrelevant and unimportant information may get included. This may cause a communication gap and thus retard the effectiveness of the communication. 4 5. No rectification – Speaking is a spontaneous process and several mistakes can happen in the process if not taken into consideration. There is no place for rectification once a message is sent. It is one way method. It is speaker centered! Rules of conveying messages orally The speaker has to be sure of five rules while conveying his message namely: 1. Clear (واضح:) • Use words and expressions that are clear to the ear! • Avoid expressions such as "The former", "the latter" and "respectively". • Allow questions from the responder to your message to ensure being understood. 2. Concise (few words) (مختصر:) • Use few words so that your important message will not be lost. (Less is more!) 3. Consistent (ثابت :) • State the message in a consistent and accurate manner all the time for all persons. Make the take home message persistent! 4. Credible/Reasonable (موثوق به /معقول:) • Make sure your message is real. Use reliable resources. Be particularly careful with internet sources. Remember, it is important that you mean what you say. 5. Courteous (Polite): • Always be polite and considerate in your wording. • Words and phrases such as: “hello", "thank you", "please", "excuse me" and "I' am sorry" are easy, effective ways to demonstrate respect. • Courtesy (politeness) is a must in the medical profession. Keep your personal feelings out of your work interactions. Avoid diminishing or embarrassing your listeners. 2. Verbal Written Communication The act of transferring and exchanging information through written letters, symbols, and words is called written communication. Written communication skills are one of the most important job skills an employee must have in any organization including health organization and health facilities. Example of Written Communication ▪ Letters and applications ▪ E-mails ▪ Memos and reports ▪ Bulletins and advertisements ▪ Brochures, handbills and leaflets ▪ Instant online messages ▪ Forms and questionnaires Advantages of Written Communication ▪ Permanent Record – The written documents can be recorded and stored permanently as proofs and evidences for future references. ▪ Accuracy – as there is a wide scope of repeated checking, and rectification ▪ Allows lengthy and complex communication – Long messages can be conveyed very easily through written communication. It also facilitates transmission of complex official orders, agendas, manuals, assignment of responsibilities and like. 5 ▪ Acceptability – The written form of information is accepted widely as it is considered authentic and removes any misunderstanding and conflict. ▪ Multitudinous and uniform approach – A large number of people can get information at the same time through written communication. Written document also ensures uniformity of the information sent to each and every person. ▪ Slow and steady process – Writing can be carried out slowly, carefully and consciously by checking and correcting the mistakes, unlike verbal communication which is more spontaneous and prone to errors. In this way, written communication becomes more effective than any other form of communication. ▪ Creative – Availability of more time enables the sender to employ creativity in their writing. This elevates the quality of communication, thus opening better and effective outcome. Disadvantages of Written Communication ▪ Time consuming – Compared to speaking, writing takes a lot of time and becomes more difficult for those who struggle with their writing proficiency. ▪ Not helpful for illiterate people – Illiterate people can neither read nor write. ▪ Lack of personal touch – Written form of communication is unable to display facial expressions, sentiments, emotions and tone of voice. Hence the messages cannot be obtained in its totality and may cause miscommunication. ▪ Delayed feedback – Feedback is a very important element of communication. It provides remarks to the senders which help them to gain confidence or understand the errors and drawbacks in the communication and do the needful adjustments. Unlike verbal communication, written communication lacks immediate feedback. ▪ Carelessness increases with length – As written communication generally includes detailed explanations and complete information so it becomes very lengthy. For this reason the receiver loses interest and tends to skim through the long paragraphs, thus missing important points. Written communication formats used in health services Written communication is used tremendously (بكثرة) in health care management. Written communication can come in many forms such as: a. Written notes between departments. b. Written communication between supervisors and employees c. Written instructions to health team members d. Patient discharge instructions. Now electronic communication is becoming standard practice. Example of these is: E-mails, Electronic lab results, Procedure and operative reports & Patient documentations. Utilities of written communication Written communication skills can help in: 1. Enhancing the image (تعزيز الصورة) of health services. 2. Laying down (إرساء) apparent principles, policies and rules for running the services. 3. Assisting in proper delegation (تفويض) of responsibilities. 4. Instructing health team and patients. 5. Improving reports of managerial issues and scientific research and findings. 6. Minimizing confusion. 6 7. Leading to better patient care. 8. Providing ready records and references. 9. Providing valid records for legal matters. 10. Determining the quality of healthcare delivery and life. Nonverbal communication Nonverbal communication is the transfer of information through the use of body language including eye contact, facial expressions, gestures and more. For example, smiling when you meet someone conveys friendliness, acceptance and openness. Everyone uses nonverbal communication all the time whether they know it or not. Nonverbal communication is dependent on seeing and analyzing physical movements as opposed to verbal communication, or the use of language to transfer information through written text, speaking or sign language. In order to understand body language and other aspects of non-verbal communication, we need to focus on our behavior during the conversation. Our body sends out signals (اشارات) no matter where we are, what we are doing or the time of the day. Our body does not know how to lie; it cannot “be turned off”. The most important thing in communication is hearing what is not said Functions of nonverbal communication (Relationship between Verbal and Non-verbal Communication) ▪ Repeating – using specific gestures to strengthen a verbal message (e.g. pointing to the object of discussion). ▪ Conflicting – when verbal and non-verbal messages within the same interaction send contradicting meaning. Conflicting messages often arise from feelings of confusion, indecision, or frustration (e.g. a friend saying how they had a great time during the party, but his voice sounds flat and his face lacks emotion). When action conflicts with verbal message, we tend to rely more on the nonverbal communication. Since much nonverbal communication is below our level of awareness, non-verbal clues are often harder to fade than verbal ones. ▪ Complementing – the accuracy of understanding information is greater when the nonverbal and verbal complement each other. Messages have been shown to be correctly recalled to a greater degree when body language affirms the verbal exchange (e.g. saying you are happy and joyfully showing it too). When we say ‘no’ and at the same time shake our head from side-to-side to reinforce the negative verbalization, we are complementing the verbal message. ▪ Substituting – at times non-verbal behaviour is used as the sole channel for communication. A simple gesture can substitute words (e.g. shaking your head to say no). When we nod our head up and down in approval of an action, we mean “yes” without using the word. Here we have substituted nonverbal sign for verbal sign. ▪ Regulating – we can use non-verbal signals to regulate speech. Called “turn-taking signals”, these gestures make it possible for us to alternate between speaking and listening (e.g. touching someone´s arm can signal that you want to talk next). ▪ Accenting – when we use non-verbal signals to emphasize our words. Good speakers will know when to use strong gestures, deliberate pauses, changes in vocal volume or speech 7 rate, etc. (e.g. someone who is verbally expressing anger may accent the message by speaking very loudly). Types on Non-Verbal Communication 1. Bodily movement 2. Touch 3. Paralanguage 4. Personal space 5. Time 6. Physical appearance 7. Silence 1- Bodily movement (facial expression, eye contact, posture, head movement and gestures) Facial expression The human face is expressive to a major extent. Through facial expressions, one can express various kinds of feelings, without saying a word. keeping an open warm fascial expression helps to build rapport with patients and colleagues. Ensure that your facial expression matches the content of your speech as this has a positive impact on building rapport, trust and confidence. Using the eyebrows, mouth, eyes and facial muscles to convey messages can be very effective when communicating both emotion and information. Unlike some forms of non-verbal communication, facial expressions are universal. The facial expressions for happiness, sadness, anger, worry, stress, anxiety, fear and surprise are the same for all the individuals, irrespective of their categories and backgrounds. You can interpret several behaviors by observing facial expressions. • An open expressions and mild smile can indicate respect. • Smiling and moistening lips may be interpreted as liking. • Hostility can be revealed by scowling (مقتطب الجبين/تجهم الوجه glaring (غاضبand clenched teeth. • Distress can be interpreted by rapid swallowing, rapid biting and wetting of lips as well as sadness expressions. Eye contact Of all the parts of the human body, the eyes are the most important for transmitting nonverbal information. Eyes are very expressive. They can reveal the inner feelings and emotions. Eye contact is frequently the first message before a spoken word. You can use eye contact to control a conversation. Example: • Looking away from someone and at the ground or your phone may convey disinterest or disrespect. • Making eye contact signals that you are listening and interested in what other person is saying. Be aware of culture differences. For example, in some cultures extended gaze convey hostility and rudeness • Eye open wide may mean amazement (surprise). • Frequent blinking may signal a fear reaction. • Pupil dilation, wide and narrowing eyes may be interpreted as liking. • Hostility can be revealed by glaring, rolling in disgust and averted gaze. 8 Posture The way you sit or stand or walk can give clues to feelings and emotions. The manner in which persons hold their bodies indicates their mood, their background and their willing to communicate. Example: • a slumped posture, can indicate tiredness. • shoulder relaxed with an upright posture, facing towards the other person indicates confidence and openness. • Leaning forward while facing the person demonstrates interest Head movement Head nod is a sign of acknowledgment. it can also be used to show that you are listening and encourage the patient to continue You can interpret several behaviors by observing head movements. • A head bow indicates respect. • A rapid nodding and tilting your head indicate liking. • Hostility can be revealed by shaking of head and tilting it. • Distress may also be revealed by shaking head. • Deceit can be interpreted by nodding when saying no and shaking the head when saying yes. Gestures While gestures vary widely across communities, they are generally used both intentionally and unintentionally to convey information to others. The word gesture refers to movement of arms and hands and occasionally the head and more rarely the whole body. Gestures serve to emphasize, clarify, or add to the verbal content of a message. Now how do we interpret gestures? • An increase in gestures suggests enthusiasm, pleasure and excitement. • Hand gestures may function as regulators in conversation. • Open hands with palms facing upwards or towards the other person suggest receptivity and respect. • Putting the thumps up: An-OK finger gestures indicate approval. • Scratching or rubbing face or nose and covering the mouth with a hand or crossing and uncrossing their legs all these may indicate stress and deceit. • Hiding hands behind one's back or sitting on the hands suggests shyness and insecurity. • Biting one's fingernails, squeezing tightly the hands or playing with a ring may be manifestations of nervousness, tension and embarrassment. • Sucking a thumb indicates stress and insecurity. • Fingertips planted spread apart on a surface display confidence and authority. • Arm spread out over chairs indicate that the person is feeling comfortable and confident. • Mirroring indicates liking. • Hostility can be revealed by shaking fists, crossed arms, hands on hips and pointing fingers. • Distress may also be revealed by hands around mouth, wringing hands (فرك اليدينjiggling legs (هزهزة الرجلand feet turned in, crossed arms and fidgeting (يعبثwith adornments حلى- سبحة).) • Leaning forward is a sign of acceptance. • Crossed feet may mean that the person is at ease. 9 • Feet tapping can indicate readiness to leave Patients, who are mechanically ventilated, are most likely to use head nods, and gestures as their primary methods of communication. 2- Touch Touching behavior is one of the most sensitive means of communication. It is described as an invisible communication system. This is because so much meaning may be transmitted by it independent of other senses. it conveys many messages and can be beneficial in giving the meaning of support and showing care and concern Example: Placing your hand on a friend’s shoulder may convey support or empathy. In situations of severe personal stress, particularly when the person feels isolated and threatened a touch can have comforting effects. Be aware of culture differences 3- Paralanguage: Vocal cues that accompany speech are called paralanguage (Para verbal communication). It is neither the language nor the signs used in communication. These cues may reveal an emotional state, attitudes towards others, social class, or origin. Paralanguage includes the non-language elements of speech, such as your talking pace, pitch, tone, volume and more. a. Pitch نبرة الصوت) :or intensity of speech. high pitch indicates feeling of joy, fear, and anger. a low pitch can indicate depression or state of calm. Women's voices are generally pitched higher than men. We may pitch our voice lower as a warning signal or as a defensive mechanism. We can lower our pitch along with the volume when we want to establish more intimate communication, or to show respect. We tend to pitch our voice higher with people we know. Changes in pitch reflect changes in emotion. Sudden shift to high pitch may reflect excitement. b. Volume: loudness can indicate confidence or aggression. soft voice can indicate helplessness or gentleness c. Pace: refers to how fast or slow a person speak s. Fast talker can convey excitement or nervousness while slow voice can indicate indifference or thoughtful. d. Tone: is the most complex vocal character. Pleasing voice are generally those that are lower in pitch and not monotone Vocal cues are associated with culture. In Arab culture, for example, speaking loudly indicates sincerity, whereas in North America it often is interpreted as aggressiveness. Voice expressions may denote different behaviors: • It can reflect respect by being silent. • It may indicate liking where the voice will have a higher pitch and warmer tone. • Hostility may be revealed with loud voice and deeper pitch. • Distress and deceit could be diagnosed by vocal cues where in both conditions one can observe shaking voice, non -words, partial words, repetitions, stumbling over words (تعثر الكلماتand higher pitch 4- Personal space: Creating or closing distance between yourself and the people around you can also convey messages about your comfort level, the importance of the conversation, your desire to support or connect with others and more. We tend to feel anxious if others invade this space; by standing too close or by touching us. There are four zones that are identified 10 a) Public zone: is 12-20 feet from the body. the communication that occurs in this zone is formal like a teacher in the classroom, within this zone we will also be comfortable with people we know only slightly or we do not at all. b) Social zone: 4-12 feet from the body. This is preferred zone for a professional interaction as it reduces the suggestion of inappropriate behavior or unintentional touching. Also for people we know only moderately well as work colleagues in a meeting. c) Personal zone: 1.5-4 feet from the body. this is the zone for friends, people we know well. and health care workers. You can easily touch the person and discuss issues in relative privacy d) Intimate zone: 0-1.5 feet from the body. this is allowed for close friends and loved ones. Being close to someone and feeling their physical presence can be very comforting when words fail. 5- Time: ovoid glancing at the clock during consultation. It suggests that you wish to finish the conversation 6- Physical appearance • Appearance messages are generally the first nonverbal messages received. • They can be used to develop judgments about people based on how they look, what they wear, and their level of attractiveness. • Your physical appearance will help you to present yours elf to others ( self- presentation). • A tall person appears to command more attention and trust than a short one • Your appearance, color, clothes, hairstyle, cosmetics and accessories may give several messages to receivers. 7- Silence: As a student of medicine, you must recognize and respect individual differences in the way they respond. The quiet person, the person with a language barrier or speech problem, the elderly and persons who lack confidence in their ability to communicate all these may resort to silence. Silence is a specific channel for transmitting and receiving messages. Silence may suggest: • Intimacy. • Evaluating and judging another's words. • Drawing attention to certain ideas or words. • Anxiety. • Fear of disclosure. • Emotional blocking and sadness. • Anger and hostility. References • Simmenroth-Nayda A, Weiss C, Fischer T, Himmel W. Do communication training programs improve students’ communication skills?–a follow-up study. BMC Res Notes. 2012;5:486. • Medical Council of Canada, University of Toronto. Medical communication skills, 2018. Available at [ http://physiciansapply.ca/commskills/introduction-to-medical- communication-skills] 19 Communication Principles PART 2 Practical activities Objective

The manner in which persons hold their bodies indicates their mood, their background and their willing to communication example: •a slumped posture, can indicate tiredness. •shoulder relaxed with an upright posture, facing towards the other person indicates confidence and openness. •Leaning forward while facing the person demonstrates interest. 14 D) Head Movement: Head nod is a sign of acknowledgment. it can also be used to show that you are listening and encourage the patient to continue. You can interpret several behaviors by observing head movements: •A head bow indicates respect. •Hostility can be revealed by shaking of head and tilting it. •Distress may also be revealed by shaking head. •Deceit can be interpreted by nodding when saying no and shaking the head when saying yes. 15 E) Gestures: The word gesture refers to movement of arms and hands and occasionally the head and more rarely the whole body. 16 Touch Touching behavior is one of the most sensitive means of communication. so much meaning may be transmitted by it independent of other senses. it conveys many messages and can be beneficial in giving the meaning of support and showing care and concern 17 Pitch: Intensity of speech. high indicates feeling of joy, fear, and anger. low indicates depression or state of calm. Women's voices are generally pitched higher than men. Changes in pitch reflect changes in emotion. Volume: loudness can indicate confidence or aggression. soft voice can indicate helplessness or gentleness. Pace: how fast or slow a person speaks. Fast talker can convey excitement or nervousness. slow voice can indicate indifference or thoughtful. Tone: is the most complex vocal character. Pleasing voice are generally those that are lower in pitch and not monotone. Paralanguage 18 Voice expressions may denote different behaviors: It can reflect respect by being silent. It may indicate liking where the voice will have a higher pitch and warmer tone. Hostility may be revealed with loud voice and deeper pitch. Distress and deceit could be diagnosed by vocal cues. 19 Personal space -Public zone:12-20 feet . The communication that occurs in this zone is formal like a teacher in a classroom, within this zone we will also be comfortable with people we know only slightly or we don’t at all. -Social zone:: 4-12 feet. This is preferred zone for a professional interaction as it reduces the suggestion of inappropriate behavior or unintentional touching. For people we only know moderately well as work colleagues in a meeting. -Personal zone: 1.5-4 feet .For friend and people we know well and for health care workers. You can easily touch the person and discuss issues in relative privacy -Intimate zone:0-1.5 feet . For close friends and loved ones. Being close to someone and feeling their physical presence can be very comforting when words fail. 20 Time 21 Physical appearance •The first nonverbal messages received is appearance • They can be used to develop judgments about people based on how they look, what they wear, and their level of attractiveness. • Your physical appearance will help you to present yourself to others (self-presentation). •Your appearance, color, clothes, hairstyle, cosmetics and accessories may give several messages to receivers. 22 Silence Intimacy. Evaluating and judging another's words. Drawing attention to certain ideas or words. Anxiety. Fear of disclosure. Emotional blocking and sadness. Anger and hostility. Silence may suggest: 23 The “SOFTEN” mnemonic is a helpful tool to remember important nonverbal behaviors: S Smile. O Open posture. F Forward lean Slight leaning forward, whether seated or standing. T Touch E Eye contact N Nod 24 Thank You
